CLASS 37 · AGES 4–5 · 40 MOVEMENT LESSONS

Sports, Movement & Play.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Forty sports, forty big moves, one active playground.

Every sport in this class is taught as ONE big move your child can try today: the soccer plant-and-swing, the basketball push-and-catch, the frog-jump landing, the pencil dive, the egg-beater float. Each card comes with its step-by-step lesson right here — what the sport is, the three ideas your child needs, the parent script, one game for the living room and, where it matters, the safety rule said out loud. The order is deliberate: the ball games a four-year-old already knows come first, then run-jump-throw athletics, the water sports, wheels and boards and ice, climbing and riding, aim and precision, the martial arts, and the mighty lift at the end.

One card a sitting is plenty — the whole class is a term of five-minute active visits. The vocabulary is the one early-years teachers use: gross motor skills, physical literacy and the fundamental movement skills — run, jump, throw, catch, kick, balance — the same words New Zealand and Australian schools teach as the heart of movement, and Canadian families know as the path to physical literacy. By the end, your child has forty named skills and forty games that grow them.

WHY MOVEMENT MATTERS

The body learns first.

Before pencils and letters come legs and lungs: active play builds the balance, grip and coordination that every classroom skill quietly borrows. This class does not train champions — it hands your child the movement words (jump, throw, glide, balance, kick) and the joy of using them, so that whatever sport your family meets next — school sports day, a swim class, a dance group — the door is already open.

And the safety rules live inside the lessons where they belong: helmets before wheels, grown-ups before water, pads before wheels roll and mats before falls. Every rule is said out loud in its lesson, every time — that repetition is the lesson.

AFTER THE LESSON

Then play the playground classics.

Class 37 teaches forty named sports skills; the school’s game rules shelf holds the games children play between them — Duck Duck Goose, Hopscotch, Simon Says, Tag, Red Light Green Light and thirty more, each with the three rules printed on its card, what you need, and one fresh twist. When today’s sport lesson ends, let the rules shelf pick the game that runs off the last of the wiggles.

THE WORDS BEHIND THE WARM-UP

Class 49 · Action Words.

Class 37 runs the sports — the drills, the games, the forty big moves; Class 49 · Action Words names the verbs underneath them: twenty-four printable action-word flashcards for ages 4–5, with run, jump, climb, push, throw, catch, kick and hit right there on the cards. Each card is right here with one way to try the move today — name it here, then go run it there.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 40 cards in Sports & Movement, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Sports & Movement. We have 40 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Soccer

    “Soccer is kicking the ball with your feet — no hands allowed! You kick it to a friend, or into the big net for a goal.”

    How: Set two chair-legs as a goal across the room and take turns kicking a soft ball through. Then add the stop: kick, run, put one foot on top of the ball — freeze it. Stopping the ball is the secret skill of every good player.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Basketball

    “Basketball is bouncing the ball with your hands and tossing it into the hoop. Bounce, bounce, throw — swish!”

    How: A laundry basket on the floor is today’s hoop. Bounce the ball five times, then drop-toss it in. Move the basket further away each round. Every catch you take is hand-eye coordination doing push-ups.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Volleyball

    “In volleyball we bump the ball up, up, up — and never let it touch the floor! Over the net to the other team, then back again.”

    How: Blow up a balloon and play keep-it-up over a string or a row of sofa cushions. Balloons hang in the air long enough for little arms to get under them — a proper bump before school even starts.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Tennis

    “Tennis is hitting the ball with a racket — tap! — over the net to your friend, and they tap it back. How many taps can we do?”

    How: Balloon or soft ball, big spoon or paddle: tap it up, let it bounce, tap again. Count your record out loud. When the taps get steady, tap it across the sofa-back "net" to a partner.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Badminton

    “Badminton uses a shuttlecock — a little feather rocket! We tap it softly and it floats over the net like a parachute.”

    How: Toss a shuttlecock (or a lightweight sponge ball) and let your child tap it back up with the flat hand first, then a junior racket. Watch how it wobbles and floats — that drift is what makes badminton feel like catching a falling leaf.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Table Tennis

    “Table tennis is ping pong! The little ball bounces on the table and we hit it with small paddles — ping, pong, ping!”

    How: Kneel at the table and bounce the ball on your paddle: how many bounces in a row? Then bounce it once on your side and tap it over the books-as-net. Fast little bounces make fast little eyes.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Baseball

    “Baseball is hitting the ball with a bat — CRACK! — then running around the bases all the way back home. Safe!”

    How: Balance a soft ball on a stool or a tee, swing a plastic bat or a rolled sock, and run your own diamond of cushions. Then trade turns: one pitches gently, one catches with the big glove. Hit, run, catch — the whole sport in a corridor.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Cricket

    “Cricket is hitting the ball with a flat bat — whack! — while the wickets stand behind you. Then we run! The other team fetches the ball.”

    How: Stand three paper-towel tubes as wickets, bowl a soft ball with a big gentle underarm roll, and swing the flat bat straight through the line. Whoever hits it gets to run; whoever fields it brings it back. Backyard cricket needs nothing else.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Rugby

    “In rugby we hold the ball with BOTH hands and run as fast as we can — but we can only pass it backwards to our friends!”

    How: Jog around the garden hugging a cushion "ball" in both arms, and on your call, pass it backwards over the shoulder to the runner behind. Forward-run, back-pass is the whole sport’s rhythm, played at four-year-old speed.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · American Football

    “This is American football — the funny egg-shaped ball! We throw it far to a friend, or hug it tight and run to the end zone. Touchdown!”

    How: Two cushions one room apart are the end zones. Take turns: hug the ball and run the "field", or point your fingers and throw it across. The oval ball flies funny — that wobble is the joke, and catching it is the skill.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Hockey

    “Hockey is pushing the puck with a stick — dribble, dribble, SHOOT! Into the goal it goes.”

    How: A sponge or paper ball is the puck, a broom or pool noodle is the stick. Dribble it around chair-cones, then shoot between the sofa-legs. On the floor nobody falls, and the dribbling skill is the same one the big ice players drill.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Lacrosse

    “Lacrosse sticks have a little net basket! We scoop the ball up, hold it in the net, and run — then throw it to a friend.”

    How: A small net bag, a scooper or even a large spoon: scoop a soft ball off the floor, jog a lap without dropping it, then toss it into a bucket. Scooping off the ground is a genuine catching skill — from below.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Handball

    “Handball is throwing the ball into the goal with your HAND — no stick, no bat, just a big strong throw!”

    How: A soft ball and a doorway or cushion goal: take three giant steps, throw with one arm, then swap and be the goalkeeper with arms up wide. Three steps, one throw, one cheer — repeat until dinner.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Golf

    “Golf is hitting the tiny ball into the tiny hole — swing slow and smooth, like brushing the grass. One… two… three taps!”

    How: A bucket, a spoon and a pom-pom: tap the pom-pom across the carpet to the bucket in as few taps as you can. Count out loud together. The counting IS the game — golf quietly teaches numbers while it teaches aim.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Athletics

    “Athletics is running, jumping and throwing — the Olympic games! Run to the line, jump as far as you can, throw it far, far away!”

    How: Chalk three stations on the pavement: a sprint line ("run fast!"), a long-jump line ("bend knees, jump!"), and a bean-bag throw ("big arm, throw!"). One minute each, big cheer, next station. That is a real athletics meet, kid-size.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Gymnastics

    “Gymnastics is balancing and rolling and making shapes with your body — arms out, one foot up… hold it, hold it… and ta-da!”

    How: Balance on one foot like a flamingo for five slow counts, then do a log roll across the bed or a mat, then hold a "star shape" — arms and legs wide. Balance, roll, shape: a full gymnastics class in the living room.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Marathon

    “A marathon is a SUPER long running race — so long it takes all day! You do not rush; you keep stepping, one foot, other foot, all the way.”

    How: Play marathon around the house or the block: instead of speed, count laps together. Ten laps earns a water break and a medal drawing. The lesson of the marathon is pacing — slow and steady really does win.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Triathlon

    “Tri means THREE! A triathlon is three races in one — first swim, then ride your bike, then run to the finish. Nobody stops in between!”

    How: Living-room triathlon: crawl across the sofa-sea (swim), ride the hobby-horse or trike loop (bike), sprint to the finish cushion (run). Announce each leg like a race commentator. Three sports, one medal.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Cycling

    “Cycling is riding your bike — helmet on first! Push the pedals round and round, and off you go down the path.”

    How: Practise the pedalling motion lying on the back, legs cycling the air — round and round, not up and down. Then helmet on, and out to the path or trike. The air-cycling game makes the real pedals feel already-known.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Swimming

    “Swimming is moving through the water — kick kick, reach reach, blow bubbles! And we NEVER swim without a grown-up.”

    How: On dry land first: lie on the tummy and do big arm circles ("windmill arms!") and fast flutter kicks. In the bath, blow bubbles with the mouth in the water. All three pieces are real swimming strokes waiting for the pool.

  24. Cards 21–30
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Diving

    “Diving is jumping into the water hands first, straight as a pencil — arms squeeze the ears, toes pointed, SPLASH (a small one!).”

    How: Practise the diver’s body on the carpet: arms up squeezing the ears, body tall, tip-toes, hold the pencil shape for three counts — then fall forward like a tree into the "water" (the sofa). The shape is the skill; the water can wait.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Water Polo

    “Water polo is throwing the ball into the goal while you float — legs kick underneath like an egg-beater, hands pass the ball to friends!”

    How: Practise the egg-beater sit: in the bath or shallow pool, sit upright and whirl the legs, arms sculling out to the sides. Then toss a soft ball to a partner — water polo passes are throws, one hand, aim at their chest.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Surfing

    “Surfing is standing on a board on the wave — paddle, paddle, POP UP! Knees bent, arms out, ride it all the way in!”

    How: Pop-up practice on the carpet: lie flat, hands under shoulders, jump the feet in and stand low in one hop — that is the surfer’s pop-up. Then balance on a cushion or a wobbly board, knees soft, arms wide. Pop up, stand tall, repeat.

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Rowing

    “Rowing is pulling the oars to move the boat — lean forward, pull back, glide! Everyone rows together, in the same rhythm: dip, pull, glide.”

    How: Sit on the floor facing a partner, hold a towel or stick between you and row: both lean forward, both pull back, counting "dip — pull — glide". In-time pulling is the actual skill of a crew — the boat only moves when everybody moves together.

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Canoeing

    “Canoeing is paddling a boat with one paddle — dip it on the left, then the right, and the canoe goes straight ahead!”

    How: Sit cross-legged on the floor holding a mop or a rolled poster as a paddle, and "paddle" a rug-boat: big reach, long pull, left side, right side. Then ask: what happens if you only paddle ONE side? (You spin in a circle!)

  30. 27
    Card 26 · Sailing

    “Sailing is letting the WIND push the boat! The big white sail catches the wind like a kite, and the boat slides across the water.”

    How: Be the boat: hold a pillow or towel "sail" to your chest and walk only where a partner blows or fans you — move toward the "wind" and you stop; angle across it and you glide. That wind-angle game is real sailing thinking.

  31. 28
    Card 27 · Skating

    “Skating is gliding on the ice — little steps first, then stand still and LET the ice carry you. Wobbly knees are doing it right!”

    How: Slipper-skate at home: socks on a smooth floor, take skating steps, then freeze and glide as far as the momentum goes. Practise the soft fall too — knees down, hands on knees, giggle. Every skater falls; good skaters fall soft.

  32. 29
    Card 28 · Skiing

    “Skiing is sliding down the snow on long boards! Tips together like a pizza slice to slow down… tips straight like french fries to go fast!”

    How: Snowplough practice in socks: slide one foot out till the heels nearly meet — the "pizza" wedge — then slide them parallel again, "french fries". Do it down a carpet slope holding your hands. The stop comes before the speed; that is the mountain’s rule.

  33. 30
    Card 29 · Curling

    “Curling is sliding a big smooth stone on the ice toward the rings — and your friends sweep the ice in front to make it go further! Sweep sweep sweep!”

    How: Kitchen curling: slide a plastic lid or a bean bag across the smooth floor toward a paper-plate target, and let the "sweepers" fan the floor in front of it with a tea towel. The sweeping genuinely helps — and that is the joke.

  34. 31
    Card 30 · Skateboarding

    “Skateboarding is riding a board on little wheels — foot up front, push with the back foot, knees bent, and roll!”

    How: Balance practice first: stand on a board (or a cushion) on carpet, feet sideways, knees soft, arms out — hold the stance for five counts. Then one gentle push on a smooth, flat surface with helmet and pads on. Stance on carpet, roll on pavement.

  35. Cards 31–40
  36. 32
    Card 31 · Climbing

    “Climbing is going UP the wall with your hands and feet — grip, reach, plan the next hold… and always, always come back down slow.”

    How: Hallway climbing wall: tape paper "holds" at climbing heights, touch them in order — red, blue, red — without lifting the feet off the floor. Then climb the real playground ladder or wall with hands and feet planning together. Up slow, down slower.

  37. 33
    Card 32 · Horse Riding

    “Horse riding is sitting on a pony and riding with gentle hands — sit tall, heels down, and hold the reins soft as holding a baby bird.”

    How: Practise the rider’s seat on a cushion-horse: sit tall, pretend reins in soft fists, heels down, and do the rising trot — up-down, up-down — while a partner counts. Gentle hands are the whole secret; ponies listen to soft fingers.

  38. 34
    Card 33 · Archery

    “Archery is shooting an arrow at the target with a bow — stand side-on, pull the string slow, aim… and let go softly. Bullseye!”

    How: Suction-cup bow or a rubber-band shooter, paper-plate target on a chair: the game is the routine, not the hit — stand side-on, draw slow, hold for one breath, release soft. Bullseye or not, a calm routine is the skill archery teaches.

  39. 35
    Card 34 · Bowling

    “Bowling is rolling the ball down the lane to knock over the pins — roll it slow along the floor… CRASH! How many fell down?”

    How: Water-bottle pins at the end of the hallway, any mid-size ball: the rule is ROLL, never throw — one hand underneath, push the ball along the floor. Then count the fallen pins together. Rolling straight is the skill; the counting is the maths class hiding inside.

  40. 36
    Card 35 · Fencing

    “Fencing is a sword game with masks on — en garde! Advance, retreat… LUNGE! The tip of your sword touches the jacket and scores a point.”

    How: Foam-sword duel with pool noodles: masks optional, manners mandatory — en garde stance (side-on, knees bent, sword up), three advances forward, three retreats back, then one big lunge at a cushion target. Footwork first, poking never at people.

  41. 37
    Card 36 · Boxing

    “Boxing is punching with big gloves — hands up protecting your face, feet planted, jab jab at the pads! We punch PADS, never people.”

    How: Grown-up holds cushions as pads: jab-jab-cross with the little fists, three rounds of thirty seconds, feet bouncing lightly. The golden rule lives on the card: pads and punching bags only, never at people, never at pets, never at walls.

  42. 38
    Card 37 · Judo

    “Judo is the GENTLE way — we grip the jacket, keep our balance, and if we fall, we fall soft like a starfish. The mat is our friend!”

    How: Break-fall practice on a bed or mat: sit, roll back, arms slap out wide — slap! Then the jacket grip: hold a partner’s sleeve and elbow, step around, both keep balance. Falling soft and gripping gentle are judo’s two first skills.

  43. 39
    Card 38 · Karate

    “Karate means ‘empty hand‘ — no weapons, just your body! Block strong, punch straight, and ALWAYS bow to your partner first.”

    How: Kata in the living room: bow, then four moves in a line — low block, middle block, high block, straight punch — counting in a big voice: ichi, ni, san, shi! (That is one, two, three, four in Japanese.) Blocks before punches, always.

  44. 40
    Card 39 · Taekwondo

    “Taekwondo is the kicking sport from Korea — front kick, side kick, roundhouse! Fast feet, strong legs, and we kick PADS, never people.”

    How: Pad-kick drill: a cushion held by the grown-up at knee height — front kick, kick, kick! Then a tiny hop and turn for the side kick. Ten kicks each leg, big count-out-loud. Kicking high asks for balance, which is why taekwondo legs are springy.

  45. 41
    Card 40 · Weightlifting

    “Weightlifting is lifting heavy things with strong muscles and a straight back — bend the knees, hold tight, lift… UP! The strongest lifters in the world do this.”

    How: Soft-barbell lift: a pool noodle with two socks for plates — feet apart, bend the KNEES (not the back), hold wide, stand tall, press overhead, big cheer, lower slow. Five lifts, then re-stack the "plates". The knees-bend rule is the whole lesson — it is how weightlifters protect their backs forever.

  46. 42
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  47. 43
    Check

    “Can you find Soccer? Now show me Diving.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  48. 44
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 40 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
